extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and advanced law students
extracted.subtask_description: Doctrines and rules for determining infringement of patents (especially combination, process, and machine patents): when making, using, selling, omitting, substituting, or combining claimed elements or steps constitutes infringement. Focuses on identity/equivalence of elements, claim scope, intent, and concerted action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination-patent infringement by same elements or equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination is infringed when the manufacture, use, or sale of any combination employs precisely the same elements or their equivalents united under the same co-operative law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "To make or use or sell a combination in which the same elements or their equivalents are united under the same co-operative law" is infringement; cases cited include Dederick v. Cassell; Dederick v. Whitman Agricultural Co.; Wheeler v. Morris. Emphasizes function/plan of co-operation and equivalence doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different combination of the same elements is not infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the same elements in a different combination (i.e., differently combined or comprising only a portion of the claimed elements) is not an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "To make or use or sell a combination in which the same elements are differently combined, or a combination which comprises only a portion of these elements... is not an infringement." Cited: Pattee v. Moline Plow Co.; Byam v. Eddy; Rowell v. Lindsay. Court looks to whether the arrangement/plan of cooperation is preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of arrangement may be infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere change of the arrangement of elements may still infringe if the operative plan or cooperative law of the patented combination is substantially the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "A change of arrangement may be infringement" — Belle Patent Button Fastener Co. v. Lucas cited. Assess whether new arrangement preserves the same plan of cooperation and function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of equivalents infringes combination claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination patent is infringed if equivalents of claimed elements are used in place of the claimed elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "That a combination is infringed if equivalents are used" (Dederick v. Whitman Agricultural Co., Wheeler v. Morris, Reay v. Rajmor). Courts apply the doctrine of equivalents to combination claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: All claimed elements must be used to infringe (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination is not infringed unless all its elements, as claimed, are used (whether essential or not).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "That a combination is not infringed unless all its elements, as they are claimed, are used..." (Boyer v. Schultz Belting Co.; American Bell Tel. Co. v. Spencer). Numerous exceptions and qualifications follow in the treatise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using less than all elements may infringe if omitted parts are new to same inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Using fewer than all claimed elements does not infringe unless the elements used were new and patentable to the same inventor (i.e., those elements are themselves the patentee's invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "That a combination is not infringed by the use of less than all its elements unless the elements used were new and patentable to the same inventor" (Thoens v. Israel). Also discussed in context of when sub-parts are separate inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of an element that performs an independent function may avoid infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: If one claimed element is omitted and that omitted element performed a function of its own not discharged by remaining elements, the omission may avoid infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "That a combination is not infringed if one of its elements is omitted where the omitted element performs a function of its own not discharged by the remaining elements" (Tobey Furniture Co. v. Colby). Courts examine whether omitted element is functionally essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of a new or unknown element may avoid infringement (new combination)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defendant substitutes an element that is new or not known at the date of the complainant's patent thereby creating a different combination, the defendants may not infringe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "if they omit entirely one of the elements... or if they substitute another which is new, or was not known at the date of the complainants' patent as a proper substitute for the omitted ingredient... the defendants do not infringe." Cases: Bo well v. Lindsay; Babcock v. Judd. Whether the substitution preserves identity of invention is fact-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution with a proper known equivalent can still avoid infringement if it makes a different combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting an element that was a known proper substitute at the relevant date may result in a different combination and avoid infringement if the old combination loses its identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text discusses substitutions that create a 'different combination' and cites Babcock v. Judd. Courts evaluate whether substitution destroys the identity of the patented combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: A combination-patent does not, by itself, protect individual old elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claiming only a combination does not protect elements of which it is composed if those elements are old; such elements are the public's property unless separately claimed as new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "A patent claiming a combination only does not protect the elements of which it is composed. If these are old, they are already the property of the public..." (Rowell v. Lindsay; Lee v. Blandy). Emphasizes necessity to distinctly claim separate inventions (elements or sub-combinations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patented element used as component of new combination can be infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of a patented invention as an element in a new combination is an infringement of the patent covering that element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "That the use of a patented invention as an element in a new combination is an infringement" (Cleveland v. Towle). If an element itself is claimed and patented, incorporation into new combinations can give rise to liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where patent claims distinct improvements, piracy of any specified improvement is infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent specifies distinct improvements (parts) comprising the combination, and any one of those improvements is pirated, the patentee may have a remedy because the patent includes those particular improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "if there be different and distinct improvements constituting parts of the combination, which are specified as such... any one of them be pirated, the same rule seems to apply as in other cases where part of an invention is pirated" (Robb). See also authorities cited (Thoens v. Israel).

rubrics_metrics.name: A patented combination used as element in a larger combination is infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patented combination is employed, either alone or with improvements or as an element in a new combination, the patent which protects it is infringed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "But where the patented combination is employed, either alone or with improvements or as an element in a new combination, the patent which protects it is infringed." Emphasis that whole patented combination enjoys protection even when used as a building block in a larger machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Useless combinations are not patentable (utility requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A useless combination, although sometimes patented in violation of the law, is not patentable subject-matter; one who improves it to make it useful may practice or patent his improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "A useless combination, although patented in violation of the law, is not patentable subject-matter... if appropriated by one who so improves or adds to it as to produce a useful combination, he may practise it or patent it as his own invention." Relevant to validity as well as infringement analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture/sale of a single element with intent to complete the combination is infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Making or selling a single element with the intent that it shall be united to other elements so as to complete a patented combination is an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "To make or sell a single element with the intent that it shall be united to the other elements, and so complete the combination, is infringement." Cases: Sax v. Hammond; Barnes v. Straus; Holmes. Intent can supply part of the act of infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seller of parts for multiple uses not liable absent concert or intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Selling elements suitable for several different patented combinations does not make the vendor a partaker in infringement unless the seller acts in concert with others or intends the parts to be used to infringe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "But to sell elements suitable for several different patented combinations does not make the vendor a partaker in the purpose to infringe the patent, and actually, by their concerted action..." Cases: Bliss v. Merrill; Maynard v. Pawling. Liability often requires proof of concerted action or specific intent to induce infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concerted action/joint infringement when parties combine efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: Where separate parties act in concert with the purpose of producing the patented combination (each supplying parts useless without the others), they may be joint infringers and tort-feasors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: Parties who, "in actual concert... actually make and sell the burner [and chimney], each utterly useless without the other... must be decreed to be joint infringers..." Courts infer concert from nature of the arrangement and distinct efforts leading to combined use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process (art) patent infringement requires performance of all claimed steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement of a patented art/process consists only in the performance of all the acts of which it is composed, or their equivalents, in the manner and in the order claimed; omission or material substitution of an essential step defeats infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "The infringement of a patented art consists only in the performance of all the acts of which it is composed or their equivalents, in the manner and in the order in which they are claimed... If one of the steps claimed as essential is omitted... the identity of the invention is destroyed and the former is not an infringement." Cases: Eames v. Andrews; Arnold v. Phelps; Cotter v. New Haven Copper Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalents in process steps can infringe
rubrics_metrics.description: A process patent can be infringed even though an equivalent is used for a claimed step; use of an equivalent step may constitute infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "That a patent for a process is infringed though an equivalent is used" (Kimball v. Hess). Courts examine whether substituted steps are equivalents in function and result; identity of product may be prima facie evidence of identity of process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different process attaining same result may not infringe
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent for a process arriving at a known result is not infringed by another process that attains the same result by a materially different mode, absent equivalence of steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "That a patent for a process arriving at a known result is not infringed by another process attaining the same result" (Anilin v. Levinstein). Courts analyze sequence, essential steps, and material differences in mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine patent infringement judged by structural law (mode operandi)
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine patent is infringed by any other machine which embodies the same structural law or mode operandi; differences in form, number, or relation of parts do not avoid infringement if the structural principle is the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "A machine is thus infringed by any other which embodies the same structural law... The model operandi, or structural law of the mechanism, is the essence of the invention." Cases: Foss v. Herbert; Cantrell v. Wallick; Grier v. Castle. 'Mere colorable alterations' should not shield an infringer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of machine's structural substance controls, not superficial variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere colorable alterations, adroit evasions, or substitution of one mechanical equivalent for another should not be allowed to avoid infringement where the accused machine performs the same service in substantially the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "Mere colorable alterations, or adroit evasions by substituting one mechanical equivalent for another... should never be allowed to protect a party." (Foss v. Herbert; Sickels v. Borden). Courts look to whether accused device 'incorporates... the substance of the invention.'
